transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. My name is Dr. Lee — I'll be talking with you today. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me?

Yeah, hi Dr. Lee. Um... they sent me here. My lieutenant made me come in. It was... well, at the station, I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern, so I was lining them up and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. 

The dispatch numbers... you know, the county just upgraded our dispatch radios last month, and they have this awful static on them now. It sounds exactly like grinding metal. My partner, he said he was gonna complain to the union rep about the headsets because they give you a headache right behind your eyes. Like this really sharp, pinching pain. I think it's the frequency they use, it just bounces off the concrete in the garage. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right, so I was doing the pattern with the airway bags, and the lieutenant came over and told me to stop. But I wouldn't step away. I couldn't. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence, so I had to keep doing it. So he sent me here. I really hope they fix those radios while I'm gone, though.
When you think back on it now, do you feel that idea—that the whole bay would 'go bad' if you stopped the pattern—was probably not realistic, or does it still feel true to you?

I mean, it still feels true because it is true. You can't just break a sequence like that, it's dangerous. It's like... well, it's like the paperwork. Everything has to be exactly right, which is why I know what they're doing. 

The injury review people, and some of the supervisors... they've been watching me through the station cameras. They put those cameras up in the bays and the breakroom back in October because someone kept stealing the French Vanilla creamer out of the fridge. My partner was so mad about that, he drinks like four cups a shift and he hates it black. But anyway, now they use those cameras to watch me. 

And they go into the system and they've been changing my triage notes after I submit them. They're altering my reports to make me look unsafe on the job. I brought it up to them, pointed out the changes, and they just brush me off and tell me it's just routine paperwork. Just routine paperwork, they say. But I know what I wrote. We use those heavy Panasonic tablets for the notes, you know? The ones with the thick rubber bumpers on the corners. The stylus is always falling out of the holder. I found one under the rear tire of rig 42 the other day, completely crushed into the concrete. But yeah, they're definitely changing my notes.
How long ago did you first start noticing these things—like the cameras watching you and the changes to your notes? Has this been going on for weeks, or longer, like several months?

It's been about two months. Yeah, the camera stuff and the paperwork, and all that stuff at the station that got everyone so alarmed... about two months. I know exactly when it started, because it was right around the time they finally swapped out the vending machines in the breakroom. 

The old machine kept eating everyone's dollar bills, and my partner lost like five bucks trying to get a bag of those Jalapeño Fritos. He kicked the glass on it so hard I thought it was gonna shatter right there. But it's that thick tempered glass, you know? Like what they use on the side windows of the rig. We had a rig window get smashed once by this guy with a tire iron on a call over on 4th street. There was glass everywhere... all over the gurney, all over the jump bag. It took us like three hours to vacuum it all out of the grooves in the diamond-plate floor in the back. 

The shop vac at the station smells exactly like burning hair when you turn it on. I keep telling the captain they need to change the filter on it, but nobody listens to me about the maintenance log. If you don't clean the filters, the motor just burns itself out.
Aside from the last two months, have you noticed any of these kinds of experiences—unusual beliefs, or trouble organizing your thoughts—going back further, say four to six months or more?

No, not really. I mean, before two months ago, everything was just... normal. I was just doing my job, running calls. It was right around the time we had that massive pile-up on the interstate, actually. You know, the one where the semi-truck jackknifed across all three lanes? 

Man, that was a mess. It was raining so hard that night, the kind of rain where the wipers on the rig are going full speed and you still can't see the taillights of the car in front of you. My partner hates driving in the rain. He always grips the steering wheel so tight his knuckles turn white. He says it's because the tread on the rear tires of rig 12 is practically bald, which is true. We wrote it up in the vehicle check like four times, but fleet maintenance is always backed up. They have this one mechanic, Gary, who works the night shift, and he's always taking these hour-long smoke breaks out by the dumpster. He smokes those little cigars, the ones with the plastic tips? They smell like cheap vanilla. 

My uncle used to smoke those when we'd go fishing up at the lake. We'd rent this little aluminum boat, and the outboard motor would always sputter and die right in the middle of the water. You had to pull the starter cord like twenty times to get it going again. My shoulder would be killing me by the end of the day. But anyway, no, I didn't notice anything strange before a couple of months ago.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or other things that other people around you didn't seem to hear?

No, I haven't heard anything like that. Just the normal stuff. I mean, my ears ring sometimes from the sirens, but that's just the job. The Q-siren on the heavy rescue trucks is the worst, it's so loud you can literally feel it vibrating in your teeth. We have these headsets in the rig to protect our hearing, but the microphone boom is always bent out of shape because someone always sits on them. 

It's usually the new guys. We had this one rookie, kid named Tyler, who sat on the main radio mic and keyed it up for like ten solid minutes while he was complaining about the cafeteria food at Memorial Hospital. The whole county dispatch heard him talking about the meatloaf. It was hilarious. They serve that meatloaf every Tuesday, and it's always swimming in this weird brown gravy that looks exactly like dirty motor oil. 

Speaking of motor oil, I really need to get the oil changed in my personal truck. I usually go to the quick lube place down on Main Street, but last time the guy there tried to upsell me on a cabin air filter for like forty bucks. I told him I can buy the exact same Fram filter at AutoZone for twelve dollars and put it in myself. It goes right behind the glovebox, you just have to pinch these two little plastic tabs together to drop the door down. If you pull too hard, the plastic hinges snap right off and then your glovebox just hangs there hitting your passenger in the knees. But yeah, no, I don't hear voices or anything like that.

Aside from the belief about the cameras and paperwork, have you noticed any changes in how well you're able to do your job, take care of daily tasks, or interact with coworkers and family over these past two months?

Yeah, I mean... things have changed a lot. I can't work the ambulance anymore. They had me doing desk duty for a bit, just handling notes and equipment checks, but even that got so... I guess they said I was unreliable, so they just took me completely off the schedule. Which is ridiculous because I know how to do an equipment check. You always check the D-cylinders for the oxygen first. You have to use that little green plastic wrench to crack the valve, and it makes this really loud hissing sound. 

My buddy Dave forgot to bleed the line once before taking the regulator off, and the O-ring shot across the apparatus bay like a bullet. We spent like an hour looking for that tiny little green rubber ring under the tires of Engine 4. Those tires are massive, by the way. They're Michelin XZYs, they cost like a thousand bucks a piece. The tread on them is so deep you could lose a whole set of keys in there. 

But yeah, I'm not on the schedule anymore. And I've mostly stopped seeing my friends, too. I just don't keep up with things at home the way I used to either. I just sit there. I was supposed to fix the leaky faucet in my kitchen, it just goes drip, drip, drip all night and echoes in the stainless steel sink. I even bought the replacement cartridge for it at Home Depot, the Moen one, but it's just sitting on the counter. I hate going to Home Depot on the weekends anyway, the parking lot is always a complete nightmare and people just leave those orange flatbed carts right in the middle of the empty parking spaces.
Over these past two months, have you been using any alcohol, drugs, or new medications/supplements?

No, no drugs or anything. I don't really drink much either, maybe a beer at a barbecue, but that's it. No new medications. I mean, I take ibuprofen sometimes for my back. You know how it is lifting the stretcher all day. The new power cots are supposed to do all the lifting for you, the Stryker ones with the battery pack? But the batteries are always dying halfway through a shift because people forget to plug them into the charging bracket in the back of the rig. 

There's this little green light that's supposed to blink when it's charging, but the contacts get all gunked up with dirt and whatever else we track into the back of the ambulance. You have to scrub them with an alcohol prep pad to get them to connect right. I swear we go through a whole box of those prep pads in a week. They smell so strong, kind of like that hand sanitizer they have everywhere at the hospital now. The foam kind? It always leaves this sticky film on your hands, and if you touch your steering wheel afterward, it gets all over the leather. My buddy Dave put one of those steering wheel covers on his truck, the ones that look like carbon fiber, but it just slides around when you try to turn. It's super dangerous, honestly. But yeah, no, no drugs or alcohol or anything like that.

I guess they said I was unreliable, so they just took me completely off the schedule. Which is ridiculous because I know how to do an equipment check. You always check the D-cylinders for the oxygen first. You have to use that little green plastic wrench to crack the valve, and it makes this really loud hissing sound. 

My buddy Dave forgot to bleed the line once before taking the regulator off, and the O-ring shot across the apparatus bay like a bullet. We spent like an hour looking for that tiny little green rubber ring under the tires of Engine 4. Those tires are massive, by the way. They're Michelin XZYs, they cost like a thousand bucks a piece. The tread on them is so deep you could lose a whole set of keys in there. 

But yeah, I'm not on the schedule anymore. And I've mostly stopped seeing my friends, too. I just don't keep up with things at home the way I used to either. I just sit there. I was supposed to fix the leaky faucet in my kitchen, it just goes drip, drip, drip all night and echoes in the stainless steel sink. I even bought the replacement cartridge for it at Home Depot, the Moen one, but it's just sitting on the counter. I hate going to Home Depot on the weekends anyway, the parking lot is always a complete nightmare and people just leave those orange flatbed carts right in the middle of the empty parking spaces.

inference.note: Ruled out F22 (delusional disorder) because the patient shows marked functional decline (removed from work, social withdrawal, neglect of daily tasks) and disorganized, tangential speech pattern, which are inconsistent with delusional disorder's requirement of relatively preserved functioning outside the delusion. Symptom duration (~2 months) with functional impairment fits schizophreniform disorder criteria (1-6 months, before ruling in/out schizophrenia).

doctor.intent: Assess for substance use or medical causes that could explain psychotic symptoms, to rule out substance-induced psychosis
doctor.question: Over these past two months, have you been using any alcohol, drugs, or new medications/supplements?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the use of alcohol, drugs, or new medications/supplements, which is not covered by any of the symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, no drugs or anything. I don't really drink much either, maybe a beer at a barbecue, but that's it. No new medications. I mean, I take ibuprofen sometimes for my back. You know how it is lifting the stretcher all day. The new power cots are supposed to do all the lifting for you, the Stryker ones with the battery pack? But the batteries are always dying halfway through a shift because people forget to plug them into the charging bracket in the back of the rig. 

There's this little green light that's supposed to blink when it's charging, but the contacts get all gunked up with dirt and whatever else we track into the back of the ambulance. You have to scrub them with an alcohol prep pad to get them to connect right. I swear we go through a whole box of those prep pads in a week. They smell so strong, kind of like that hand sanitizer they have everywhere at the hospital now. The foam kind? It always leaves this sticky film on your hands, and if you touch your steering wheel afterward, it gets all over the leather. My buddy Dave put one of those steering wheel covers on his truck, the ones that look like carbon fiber, but it just slides around when you try to turn. It's super dangerous, honestly. But yeah, no, no drugs or alcohol or anything like that.

inference.note: No substance or medication use reported, ruling out substance-induced psychosis. Symptom duration remains at 2 months with persistent disorganized speech, persecutory delusions, and functional decline, consistent with schizophreniform disorder (duration <6 months) rather than brief psychotic disorder (<1 month) or schizophrenia (>6 months).

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome in. My name is Dr. Lee — I'll be talking with you today. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me?
